interviewQuestions.question: How would you detect a corrupted message as cheaply as possible?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd first ask whether retransmission is an option, since that decides whether I need detection alone or full correction — a much more expensive redundancy budget.

Assuming retransmission is cheap (a normal network setting), I'd reach for a **CRC** rather than a plain parity bit or naive checksum. A single parity bit is nearly free but blind to any even number of flips — a real risk with burst errors. A CRC costs a bit more (a few extra bytes, cheap polynomial-division hardware) but reliably catches all single-bit errors and the overwhelming majority of realistic burst-error patterns, which is exactly why Ethernet and most storage formats use it instead of parity.

Concretely, I'd append a CRC-32 (or similar) to the message, have the receiver recompute it, and trigger a retransmission request on mismatch — cheap to compute, cheap to check, and it doesn't need to spend bandwidth on full error-correction redundancy since a resend covers the rest.

I'd only reach for actual error-correcting codes (Hamming, Reed-Solomon) if retransmission were impossible or too slow — e.g. deep-space links or read-only storage.

**Testing:** whether you can pick the right redundancy/cost trade-off for detection-only versus correction, rather than reaching for the strongest code by default.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Cheap corruption detection with CRC
